source.title: [Interim research report] Taking features out of superposition with sparse autoencoders

page_placements.theme: Cross-seed and cross-size reproducibility of SAE features

record.file_problem: none; the full post and comments are present
record.tranche_reason: It compares SAE dictionaries of different sizes using mean max cosine similarity, a different measure of whether larger and smaller dictionaries have related features. It does not measure whether child features partition a parent feature's inputs.
record.gate_note: The eligible results are the cross-dictionary MMCS comparisons in Figures 10 and 13. The toy-data MMCS against known ground-truth features measures recovery, not whether features in one dictionary split into features in another. Dead-neuron and loss-stickiness results address hyperparameter selection, not the claimed split pattern.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. Its cross-dictionary mean max cosine similarity (MMCS) asks whether each smaller-dictionary feature has one close match in a larger dictionary. That cannot show a coarse feature being replaced by several finer features covering its inputs, nested families, absorption, or decomposition versus novel latents. In the toy data the ground truth is fixed at G features. The authors expect larger dictionaries to relearn the same features plus dead or duplicate units, not splits. The post only speculates that too-small dictionaries learn combinations of correlated features, which is not measured. MMCS is a related but different construct, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but add: a simple L1 sparse autoencoder recovers ground-truth features in toy data and is robust to 1-8x overparameterization; the L1 penalty interacts with dictionary size. On the language model, results differ from the toy data and are too uncertain to fix a dictionary size. The authors give very weak, tentative evidence of over 100,000 features. In a later comment the author says the language-model SAEs were likely undertrained.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a single-layer ReLU autoencoder with an L1 penalty and unit-norm decoder features. The relevant comparison is cross-dictionary MMCS; the study does not test input coverage or parent-to-child feature splits.
record.method_sensitivity: The real-model MMCS varies with dictionary size and L1 penalty. The authors say the elevated-similarity pattern may continue beyond the largest tested dictionary, so the endpoint is unresolved.

fits_no_version.finding: Toy data: features of the right-sized dictionary have near-identical matches in larger dictionaries. Peak cross-size MMCS is at the true dictionary size and optimal L1. Ground-truth recovery stays high from 1x to 8x overparameterization, with MMCS slowly decreasing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With a fixed set of independent ground-truth directions, larger SAEs relearn the same features (plus dead or duplicate units) rather than splitting them.

fits_no_version.finding: Second MLP layer of a 31M-parameter language model: MMCS between dictionaries of different sizes never exceeds ~0.4. The authors say features of different-sized dictionaries are often quite different, possibly because of noise or undertraining.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features learned on language-model activations are not stable one-to-one across dictionary sizes.

record.code_released: not stated; the authors say code would be included in a final research report
record.problems: The report describes the language-model results as interim and uncertain. The real-model cross-dictionary MMCS is low, results are presented in plots without reported uncertainty estimates, and the authors identify possible undertraining, noisy activations, and an insufficiently large dictionary as unresolved explanations.
record.rows_left_out: No other eligible cross-dictionary results were reported. The toy-data ground-truth recovery plots, loss results, and dead-neuron counts were not included because they do not measure the claimed relation between features in smaller and larger dictionaries.

untested.parts: Whether a coarse feature is replaced by several finer features that cover its inputs and lie near its direction.
All: no large model and no open SAE release.
All: no feature families or concept hierarchy.
All: no parent/child firing or absorption analysis.
All: no decomposition of larger latents into smaller ones and no count of novel latents.
All: no comparison of training objectives. The toy data has correlated features, but splitting is not measured.

record.verdict_notes: This 2022 interim report predates the feature-splitting work and does not address splitting. In a comment, the author remarks that SAE features are "probably too granular". That is an opinion, not a result. MMCS ignores redundant or split copies, which the authors themselves note, so it cannot register splitting. The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its supports/limits_scope labels on V1 should be dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure whether a coarse feature is replaced by several more specific features or whether those features partition the coarse feature's inputs.
No test of nested feature families or a hierarchy of concepts.
No parent-child firing or absorption analysis.
No analysis of larger latents as combinations of smaller latents or of novel latents.
No comparison of SAE objectives, including Matryoshka SAEs, or test of whether splitting is an objective artifact.

rows.subject: toy data
rows.operation_detail: Compared each learned dictionary with larger learned dictionaries using mean max cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Mean max cosine similarity between dictionaries of different sizes; where a size had multiple larger dictionaries, the study averaged those MMCS values.
rows.value: The authors report that the empirical result matches the predicted pattern: similarity peaks where the smaller dictionary is the right size and compares it with larger dictionaries; numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes an elevated-similarity pattern but gives no numerical MMCS values. This tests cross-dictionary directional similarity, not input partitioning or feature specificity.
rows.check: Toy-data cross-dictionary MMCS (Fig. 10) measures one-to-one directional match, not splitting or input coverage. The authors' predicted pattern for oversized dictionaries is duplicates or dead units, not finer features. It is also a hyperparameter-selection heuristic, and no values are given in the text.

relation.reason: This 2022 post predates the splitting term. It argues that too-small dictionaries learn combinations of correlated features and too-large ones add dead or repeated units, but it measures neither.

tranche.reason: Cross-dictionary MMCS averages one-to-one best matches and cannot show a coarse feature being replaced by finer features covering its inputs. The toy data use independent random ground-truth directions with no hierarchy, and the LM result is unresolved (authors suspect noise or undertraining). No version is tested, so the reader's T2 is not supported.

source_check.notes: This is an interim report by an author shared with an original source. It has no splitting measure. The ~0.4 LM MMCS is for layer 1 only, and in a later comment the author says the LM SAEs were probably undertrained. Toy MMCS values (Fig. 10) are given as a pattern, not as numbers.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: toy data, varied dictionary sizes and L1 penalties
reader_labels.reason: The authors report the expected elevated cross-dictionary similarity pattern in the toy data, supporting a relation between dictionaries of different sizes on this synthetic dataset; this does not establish feature splitting or input coverage (r1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Cross-dictionary MMCS stays at or below ~0.4 and the authors report that features in different-sized dictionaries are often quite different, limiting how consistently this relation holds in the tested real-model setting (r2).
